extracted.intended_audience: general public, policymakers, journalists, and stakeholders concerned with public comment integrity and net neutrality
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and assess the integrity of public comments submitted to government rulemakings (notice-and-comment), including detecting fraud (impersonation, fabricated responses, automation) and applying recommended procedural, technical, and legal reforms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obtain valid consent before submitting comments on behalf of an individual
rubrics_metrics.description: Advocacy groups to take steps to ensure they have obtained valid consent from an individual before submitting a comment or message to the government on their behalf.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourages organizations to verify and document that individuals authorized submission of comments in their name rather than allowing third parties or lead generators to submit without consent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hold advocacy groups and their vendors accountable for submitted comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies and legislatures that manage electronic systems that receive comments and messages to hold advocacy groups and their vendors more accountable for the comments they submit on behalf of individuals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accountability can include auditing, vendor oversight, contractual requirements, and enforcement actions when organizations or their vendors submit deceptive or unauthorized comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strengthen laws to deter deceptive and unauthorized comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Lawmakers to strengthen laws to deter the submission of deceptive and unauthorized comments to the government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislative changes are recommended to increase deterrence and enable prosecution or civil remedies for deceptive mass-comment campaigns (astroturfing, impersonation, fraud).

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt technical safeguards to protect against unauthorized bulk submissions using automation
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies to adopt technical safeguards to protect against unauthorized bulk submissions using automation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technical measures include systems and controls to detect and block bulk or automated comment submissions, rate-limiting, CAPTCHA, provenance tracking, or other backend protections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Astroturfing defined and identified as deceptive practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Astroturfing: disguising an orchestrated, paid campaign as a grassroots effort, to create a false appearance of genuine, unpaid public support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that campaigns funded by industry or other actors that present paid or organized outputs as spontaneous public support are deceptive and distort policymaking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fabrication and impersonation of consumers' responses
rubrics_metrics.description: Lead generators that were hired to enroll consumers in campaigns instead simply fabricated consumers’ responses; more than 8.5 million fake comments impersonated real people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fabricated responses and impersonation are indicators of inauthentic comments; systems and investigations should look for submissions that purport to be from real individuals but were never authorized or produced by them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of fictitious identities and automated software to submit comments
rubrics_metrics.description: The FCC received another 9.3 million fake comments supporting net neutrality that used fictitious identities. Most of these were submitted by a single person — a 19-year-old college student using automated software.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Automated submissions and fictitious identities are common modes of fraud; detection should include analysis for automated patterns, single-origin mass submissions, and fabricated identity fields.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of lead generators employing prizes and sweepstakes to lure participants
rubrics_metrics.description: Broadband industry engaged commercial lead generators that used prizes — like gift cards and sweepstakes entries — to lure consumers to their websites and join the campaign; nearly every lead generator instead fabricated responses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incentive-based enrollment mechanisms are a risk factor for later fabrication; oversight of third-party lead generators and transparency about recruitment methods are recommended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-campaign bulk fraud and contamination of multiple proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: Three lead generation firms involved in the net neutrality campaigns had also worked on more than 100 other, unrelated campaigns. In nearly all of these advocacy campaigns, the lead generation firms engaged in fraud, generating more than 1 million fake comments for other rulemaking proceedings and more than 3.5 million fake digital signatures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigations should consider vendor histories and cross-campaign patterns; fraud by vendors can infect many different proceedings and legislators' mailstreams.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enforcement remedies: corporate agreements, reforms, penalties, and disgorgement
rubrics_metrics.description: Agreements with Fluent, Opt-Intelligence, and React2Media require the companies to adopt comprehensive reforms in future advocacy campaigns and pay more than $4.4 million in penalties and disgorgement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remedies for detected fraud include negotiated corporate agreements requiring future reforms, monetary penalties, disgorgement, and obligations to change practices; these can serve both punitive and preventative functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patterns and hallmarks of fake comment campaigns
rubrics_metrics.description: The report highlights common hallmarks of fraudulent campaigns: fabricated responses, impersonation of real people, fictitious identities, high-volume submissions, and use of automation or unauthorized bulk submissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these hallmarks to triage and investigate suspect comment sets—e.g., unusually high volumes from particular vendors or identical/form-based content, submissions linked to lead-generator recruitment, or rapid bursts of entries consistent with automation.
